title: How a GOP redistricting 'dummymander' in North Carolina backfired by 2 seats

body:
How a GOP redistricting 'dummymander' in North Carolina backfired by 2 seats   In North Carolina, Republican lawmakers redrew voting maps, aiming to  gain one seat in Congress. Instead, they lost two seats, in a classic example of what political scientists call a "dummymander."

    
        Politics
    


      
                  
            November 21, 20267:40 AM ET
         
      
   
                              By                
            


      
      
How a GOP redistricting 'dummymander' in North Carolina backfired by 2 seats 

    
            
                
                Transcript
            
        
                Download
                
                
                    
                        
                            
                            Embed
                        
                        
                            <iframe src="https://www.npr.org/player/embed/nx-s1-6044778/nx-s1-10014639" width="100%" height="290" frameborder="0" scrolling="no" title="NPR embedded audio player">
                        
                    
                
                
                  
                    
                    Transcript
                  
                
        
    




      In North Carolina, Republican lawmakers redrew voting maps, aiming to  gain one seat in Congress. Instead, they lost two seats, in a classic example of what political scientists call a "dummymander."   


    
        
          Transcript
        
    SCOTT SIMON, HOST:  Politicians across the country redrew political maps last fall to try to win congressional seats. Now we know that this gerrymandering, mostly led by Republicans, was overwhelmed by a Democratic wave. New Republican-drawn maps in Ohio saw voters elect three more Democrats. And in eastern North Carolina, Republicans redrew a pair of congressional districts in an effort to win both instead of one, but Democrats won both seats. It's an example of what political scientists call a dummymander. The North Carolina Newsroom's Adam Wagner reports from Raleigh.ADAM WAGNER, BYLINE: Last fall, Republican state Senator Ralph Hise told a Senate committee the revamped map would combat gains Democrats were poised to make elsewhere by giving Republicans one more U.S. House seat.(SOUNDBITE OF ARCHIVED RECORDING)RALPH HISE: The end result is a congressional map that should perform to elect 11 Republicans.WAGNER: Republicans moved six GOP-leaning counties along North Carolina's coast out of the 3rd Congressional District and into the 1st. They hoped that would help a Republican beat incumbent Democratic Congressman Don Davis in a seat widely considered to be North Carolina's most competitive district.To keep the sizes of the districts even, they moved four purple counties into the state's 3rd Congressional District. That weakened the advantage held by incumbent Republican Congressman Greg Murphy. His Democratic opponent, Raymond Smith, is a former state legislator, educator and U.S. Army veteran. He lives in one of the counties lawmakers moved.RAYMOND SMITH: Prior to that gerrymander, I was in the 1st Congressional District. Congressman Davis was my congressman.WAGNER: Smith says he hadn't considered running for Congress until the new map was finalized. With the changes, he came to believe a Democrat could win in the 3rd District.SMITH: It certainly piqued our interest.WAGNER: Murphy, the incumbent, also thought the district was in play.GREG MURPHY: It made us the weakest Republican district in the state.WAGNER: Murphy says the new map shifted the 3rd District's priorities. The district has historically been coastal, and he spent considerable time developing expertise on those issues.MURPHY: There was obviously a radical change with those maps.WAGNER: Murphy seriously considered staying with the coastal counties and running in the new 1st Congressional District. But he stayed in the 3rd, where voters elected Smith by about 260 votes.Meanwhile, the Democratic candidate in the first district also won. Incumbent Don Davis defeated the GOP's Laurie Buckhout in a 2024 rematch. Vote totals from the counties that Republicans shifted suggest that under the previous map, Davis and Murphy likely would've both won reelection. That makes the new map a dummymander.CHRIS COOPER: You almost couldn't draw up a better textbook example than what they did in the 1st and the 3rd.WAGNER: That's Western Carolina University political scientist Chris Cooper.COOPER: It did not touch any other district in the state, right? Twelve districts were untouched. They said the point of it out loud - to get Don Davis out of office, to get another Republican in and to hold on to the 3rd. And we can see they failed, and they failed.WAGNER: Cooper thinks the blue wave that swept across the country played a key role in Democrats winning both of these redrawn districts. That doesn't mean it's a permanent shift. A textbook dummymander in 2026 could, he says, turn out to be a successful gerrymander for the GOP as soon as 2028.For NPR News, I'm Adam Wagner in Raleigh.

title: Medicare looks a bit different in 2027, so don't miss open enrollment
description: A counselor, right, helps a client throu
body:
A counselor, right, helps a client through the Medicare signup process at a resource center for older adults in Sunrise, Florida. Medicare open enrollment season started Oct. 15 and ends Dec. 7.
                
                    Joe Cavaretta/South Florida Sun Sentinel/Tribune News Service via Getty Images
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Joe Cavaretta/South Florida Sun Sentinel/Tribune News Service via Getty Images

   
   Annual open enrollment is underway for Medicare, the federal program that provides health insurance to roughly 70 million people. The coverage choices are complex and often consequential.   Open enrollment runs through Dec. 7. The plan you choose takes effect on Jan. 1, for the full calendar year.   
   Build-your-own Medicare menu   Medicare provides health insurance to people 65 or older, as well as to some younger people with disabilities or certain health conditions. But it isn't one plan. It's more like a build-your-own-insurance menu.   Roughly half of beneficiaries are enrolled in traditional Medicare, which consists of Parts A and B. Administered by the federal government, the plan covers hospital stays, skilled nursing care, doctor visits, outpatient care, and preventive screenings. Enrollees can typically see any healthcare provider who accepts Medicare, and they rarely need approval for diagnostic tests, such as MRIs and CT scans. However, there's no cap on out-of-pocket expenses in traditional Medicare, and it doesn't cover most prescriptions or dental, vision, or hearing services.   
      As a result, most traditional Medicare enrollees buy extra coverage from private insurance companies under Medicare Part D, the prescription drug plan. Some also buy a Medigap policy that covers the costs traditional Medicare leaves behind, such as deductibles, copayments, and coinsurance.   Medicare Advantage   This year, the other half of Medicare beneficiaries opted for privately offered, all-in-one managed-care plans known as Medicare Advantage, usually including prescription drug coverage, dental, and vision. The drawbacks are smaller networks and a greater likelihood that treatments and medications will require prior authorization. Like beneficiaries in traditional Medicare, Medicare Advantage participants also pay Part B premiums.   "People really need to do their research before they enroll in Medicare, because there are trade-offs," said David Lipschutz, a co-director at the Center for Medicare Advocacy.   The hassle saves money   Every fall, insurers that offer Part D and Advantage plans send enrollees a critical document known as an Annual Notice of Change. It's a cheat sheet outlining what will be different in the following year: premiums, deductibles, covered drugs. Consumer advocates and Medicare experts say people sometimes make the costly mistake of throwing it out or filing it away without reading it. Can't find it? Call the insurer and ask for another copy.   
   The Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services projects that the average Part D premium will increase less than $1 a month for a standalone prescription drug plan, describing the market as stable. But that average doesn't tell the whole story. An analysis by KFF, the health policy research nonprofit that includes KFF Health News, found that enrollees who stay in their prescription drug plan will see a 50% increase on average, from $34 to $51. About 10.4 million people could pay higher premiums, not including higher deductibles and coinsurance costs.   
            
        
            
            
            
        


    
        
                About 4 million people are in Medicare Advantage plans that won't be offered in 2027. If they do nothing, they'll be automatically enrolled in traditional Medicare.
                
                    Jenny Kane/AP
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Jenny Kane/AP
    

   
   Some beneficiaries who didn't have to pay monthly premiums in recent years will begin paying for prescription drug Part D coverage in 2027. While that change follows the 2025 introduction of federal caps on out-of-pocket drug expenses, it comes as the Trump administration is ending temporary federal subsidies that helped keep premiums down. The cap on out-of-pocket expenses for prescription drugs in 2027 will be $2,400, a total enrollees can opt tospread out over the course of the year.   Juliette Cubanski, who directs the Program on Medicare Policy at KFF, said people who don't shop around could be leaving money on the table.   "It is worth it to avoid any unpleasant surprises in the form of either higher premiums or higher cost sharing for covered services in 2027," she said.   Some plans no longer offered   An estimated 4.3 million people now have to look for a new Medicare Advantage or prescription drug plan after private insurers left the market. Those who want to stay in Medicare Advantage must select new coverage, or they'll be moved to traditional Medicare automatically. For those shopping for a new plan, low monthly premiums may be appealing, but it's important to read the fine print and add up the other costs.   "There are going to be, often, increases in cost sharing and copays, increases in out-of-pocket caps, and reductions in the scope of some of the extra benefits that Medicare Advantage plans provide," Lipschutz said.   
   So ask: Is my prescription covered? Is my pharmacy preferred? Is my doctor in-network? What does the dental benefit actually cover?   And pay attention to the out-of-pocket maximum for the Advantage plans, Cubanski said, so you know how much you might have to shell out in 2027.   "Look at that dollar value specifically," she said.   For those moving to traditional Medicare, it won't come with a drug plan, so enrollees must sign up for a new Part D plan if they want most prescriptions covered. Enrollees who miss that step when they are first eligible may not have drug coverage for the coming year, and they may face a late-enrollment penalty on their monthly premiums for life.   When selecting a drug plan, enrollees must also tell their insurer how they want to pay, either by getting a bill in the mail or by having the cost deducted from their Social Security. If you don't pick a payment plan, you could get dropped from coverage.   
   If enrollees elect to leave their Medicare Advantage plans for traditional Medicare within their first year of joining Medicare, they have a guaranteed right to buy a Medigap plan, with no health screening. After that, all bets are off: Insurers in most states can turn enrollees down or charge more because of a health condition. Connecticut, Maine, Massachusetts, and New York are exceptions.   Enrollees whose Advantage plans have not been renewed — and haven't been consolidated into another plan — can switch to traditional Medicare and buy a Medigap policy without a health screening, but they need to act before March.   For shopping help, think "SHIP"   Medicare experts advise enrollees to write down all their prescription drugs, as well as any procedures planned in the next year, such as a joint replacement or dental work, to help them decide which plan will cover their needs. Call a favorite doctor's office to see whether they are in-network for the plans being considered. Remember that brokers might earn commissions, especially on Advantage plans, and might not represent every plan.   
   For unbiased help, every state has a federally funded State Health Insurance Assistance Program that offers free plan counseling specific to your situation, in person and over the phone. To get help, go to the website at shiphelp.org/open-enrollment, email info@shiphelp.org, or call the SHIP National Technical Assistance Center at 877-839-2675.   A SHIP counselor can also help enrollees apply for benefits that help pay for Medicare premiums and prescription drug costs, such as the Medicare Savings Programs and Medicare Part D Extra Help.   KFF Health News is a national newsroom that produces in-depth journalism about health issues and is one of the core operating programs at KFF — the independent source for health policy research, polling, and journalism.

title: A second judge blocks Trump's arch, saying it's unlikely to succeed in court
description: President Trump holds up a model of his
body:
President Trump holds up a model of his proposed triumphal arch at a White House event in Oct. 2025. Two different federal judges have ruled against it this week.
                
                    John McDonnell/AP
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        John McDonnell/AP
    

   
   A federal judge in Virginia plans to issue a preliminary injunction blocking President Trump's triumphal arch indefinitely.   District Judge Leonie Brinkema said during a Friday hearing that she would grant the request of the county board of Arlington, Va., which sued over the arch in October. Democracy Forward, the nonprofit representing the plaintiffs, confirmed the ruling in a statement shared with NPR.   
   "We are pleased that the court has recognized the irreparable harm that will come to people who live and work in Arlington and stopped the massive vanity project while our case is heard and considered by the court," said senior counsel Kate Talmor.   Justice Department spokesperson Matthew Nies told NPR it will appeal the decision immediately.   The 250-foot arch would be built in Memorial Circle, which is part of D.C. but sits on the Virginia side of the Potomac River, a short distance from both Arlington National Cemetery and Ronald Reagan Washington National Airport, both in Arlington.   
   Arlington County has argued that the arch would "cause significant harm" to its residents in multiple ways, including increasing noise and air pollution and "clogging thoroughfares needed for emergency transport services." And it said an arch that doubles as a military complex — as Trump has suggested — would pose public safety risks and require additional county resources to manage.   Arlington also argues the arch would disrupt historic sightlines between Arlington National Cemetery and D.C.'s National Mall, and pose logistical challenges for the roughly 24 to 27 funerals the cemetery holds every weekday. The county also has concerns about air and road traffic, saying construction-related delays could cause more accidents and disrupt emergency vehicles far beyond the traffic circle.   "In the last 60 days, Arlington police, fire, and emergency units have responded to approximately 200 incidents in the area surrounding the Circle, including traffic stops and assisting with unconscious persons within Arlington National Cemetery," they wrote. "And the visitors the Arch is intended to attract will increase demand for those same emergency services."   
   The plaintiffs, like many critics of the arch, accused the Trump administration of rushing through federally mandated environmental reviews and failing to consider alternatives. The National Park Service has defended the federal review process — which ended in approval earlier this month — and said building the arch somewhere else would defeat its purpose.   "The County brings this lawsuit to halt the agency's feverish pace toward construction of the Arch and to ensure that the 'hard look' mandated by [the National Environmental Preservation Act] is completed before the agency commences disruptive and harmful ground-disturbing activities," the plaintiffs wrote last month.   
   NPR has reached out to the White House for comment. Spokesperson Davis Ingle told NPR earlier this week that the administration will "continue making the case for this beautiful and fitting monument and are confident we will be fully vindicated as this litigation proceeds."   Brinkema, an appointee of President Clinton, is the second judge to rule against the arch this week.   On Wednesday, D.C. District Judge Tanya Chutkan extended a restraining order that prevents the Trump administration from breaking ground through Dec. 3 while she considers the underlying legal arguments.   
   That case was brought earlier this year by a group that includes Vietnam War veterans and was joined by the governments of D.C. and Virginia last month. Nine Kennedy family members moved to get involved last week.   Friday's ruling goes even further, preventing construction while Arlington's legal challenge plays out.   And Brinkema suggested that Arlington is likely to prevail. The judge said in court that she didn't see "any way" the government could win the case on the merits.   She reiterated that the project lacks congressional approval, which the Trump administration has not sought. It argues that the arch is covered by a 1925 law authorizing a pair of much shorter columns at that same location, which were never built. Both judges have frowned upon that argument.   
   "It hurts your credibility with the court by focusing on that," Brinkema told lawyers Friday, according to Reuters.   Brinkema also called it a "rushed job," and seemed to find the government's analysis of the structure's environmental and economic impact inadequate, particularly concerning the impact of construction cranes — which the government has said would be taller than the arch itself — on airspace.   The Federal Aviation Administration has said the arch would not pose a hazard to aircraft as long as it is lit a certain way, including with a controversial eternal flame on top. But aviation safety experts are concerned that the structure would add an additional layer of risk to an already notoriously complicated airspace. They say that's especially true if it has any military capabilities, which were not included in the FAA's analysis.

title: Trump orders federal contractors to check with White House before responding to Congress
description: President Trump speaks at a news confere
body:
President Trump speaks at a news conference in the James Brady Press Briefing Room of the White House, Friday, Nov. 20, 2026, in Washington.
                
                    Jacquelyn Martin/AP
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Jacquelyn Martin/AP
    

   
   NEW YORK (AP) — President Donald Trump is directing federal contractors and subcontractors to consult with his administration about inquiries they receive from Congress and to withhold any communications that the White House considers privileged, according to a new executive order.   The companies must also coordinate with the White House and U.S. agencies on "appropriate responses" to any such requests, the order issued late Friday says. If they fail to comply, the White House warns their contracts could be terminated and their future work with the federal government suspended.   The order is the Republican administration's latest effort to resist what are expected to be wide-ranging and aggressive oversight efforts from Democrats when they take over Congress in January. Democrats have made government contracts one of their top investigative targets, noting that federal money has been flowing to companies linked with Trump's family, particularly at the Pentagon.   
   White House officials have already begun taking steps to exert more control over how agencies and officials respond to congressional requests, anticipating there will be a flood of investigations initiated by Democrats.   Trump's counsel, Will Scharf, told federal agencies on Monday that they must seek approval from his office and the White House's Office of Legislative Affairs before agreeing to appear before Congress. Scharf also suggested in a recent letter to Rep. Robert Garcia of California, the top Democrat on the House Oversight Committee, that some congressional investigations may amount to "blatant criminality."   Garcia sent letters this week directing members of Trump's family and top administration officials to preserve documents. Scharf sought to dismiss the requests, noting in a letter to Democratic lawmakers that they are not yet in the majority and cannot compel compliance.   Responding to the new executive order, Garcia said it was part of the administration's "blatant attack on Congress' constitutional right to conduct oversight." He said that despite efforts to impede investigations, "we're just getting started."   In a fact sheet, the White House framed the new requirements as "protecting executive privileges from congressional overreach," arguing that some congressional leaders have tried to intrude on executive branch privileges by "harassing private companies that contract with the federal government."   
   Presidents of both parties have long used executive privilege to resist congressional inquiries, but the claims can set up messy, protracted legal fights as parties dispute whether it applies. Executive privilege allows the president to keep information from the courts, Congress and the public to protect the confidentiality of White House deliberations, but the protection is far from absolute.   The latest executive order applies to all contractors and subcontractors, a universe of tens of thousands of businesses.

title: The latest from Trump's press conference
description: President Trump gave a wide-ranging press conference following his historic trip to Asia where he met with Chinese President Xi and Russian Pre
body:
President Trump gave a wide-ranging press conference following his historic trip to Asia where he met with Chinese President Xi and Russian President Putin.   

    
        
          Transcript
        
    AILSA CHANG, HOST:  President Trump returned to Washington after his three-day trip to Asia and took questions from the White House today. The trip included the first ever three-way meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin. But there was little in the way of agreements on key global issues.(SOUNDBITE OF ARCHIVED RECORDING)PRESIDENT DONALD TRUMP: The United States entered this trip from a position of unmatched economic and diplomatic strength.CHANG: Well, all of this raises questions about the staying power of Trump's America-first approach and America's future role in the world. Joining us now is NPR White House correspondent Franco Ordoñez, who is in the room, and we have NPR national security correspondent Greg Myre. Hello to both of you.FRANCO ORDOÑEZ, BYLINE: Hello.GREG MYRE, BYLINE: Hi, Ailsa.CHANG: All right. So, Franco, did the president make any news in this press conference?ORDOÑEZ: Yeah, I mean, not really. I mean, it was really a very meandering talk, starting off with highlights of his first two years in office. And then he probably spent about 30 minutes talking about his time abroad and, you know, recounting his relationship with Xi and Putin. He did say, though, that he and Xi had made some agreements about putting in guardrails - that's the word he used - with artificial intelligence, which he calls super intelligence. Here he is there.(SOUNDBITE OF ARCHIVED RECORDING)TRUMP: It's not artificial intelligence. It's not artificial. It's super. Problem is, it may be too super. So President Xi and I agree that we're going to do some joint guardrails, the two of us, 'cause there really is no third place.ORDOÑEZ: Now, of course, details are scarce, but the idea of guardrails is notable because Trump has pretty - previously, at least, been pretty allergic to any restrictions on developing AI. I mean, he has repeatedly said he's wanted to maintain a U.S. advantage over China.CHANG: Right. OK, well, Greg, Trump had some things to say about chip sales to China and the whole Nvidia fallout, right? What struck you about his answers there?MYRE: Yeah, I mean, Trump says he wants the U.S. to keep the lead in AI, as Franco just noted. And he also said he won't allow U.S. companies to build AI data centers outside the U.S. However, Trump is the one allowing Nvidia to sell advanced chips to China. Nvidia's Jensen Huang lobbied Trump last year and persuaded the president to allow these sales. And just yesterday, the House Foreign Affairs Committee released a list of requests this year by Nvidia and another chipmaker, AMD, to sell chips to Chinese company - companies. As of May this year, the Trump administration approved the sale of nearly 900,000 advanced chips, and they include big names like Alibaba and Tencent. And those two companies are also on a Pentagon list of Chinese firms that are linked to the Chinese military. So what does Trump actually want here? Does he want Nvidia to keep selling those chips to China, or does he want to block those sales?CHANG: Good questions. Well, Trump was also asked about the whole change in leadership over cybersecurity, right? What did we learn there?MYRE: Yeah, Trump fired the White House Cybersecurity Director Sean Carncross, and at the press conference today, he said, I don't think that person was good enough. Now, he's being replaced by Kirsten Davies, who's been the chief information officer at the Defense Department. And this is certainly an important position, but it's a policy position, not a hands on operational position.The agency that's really important here is CISA, the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency, which deals with election security and protecting government networks from cyberattacks. And this agency has not had a director since Trump became president almost two years ago. Now, as it happens, Trump's nomination to lead the agency, Michael LoSapio, had a Senate confirmation hearing yesterday. He was grilled by Democratic senators. He was asked who won the 2020 presidential election. He refused to answer. He was asked if the Capitol was attacked on January 6, 2021, and he said he didn't think it was an attack. So it's not clear that he'll be confirmed, but whoever winds up in this position will be in charge of election security in 2028.CHANG: Interesting. OK, Franco, back to this meeting with Xi and Putin, which was designed to demonstrate American power, right? Do you think it also may have opened the door for allies to turn away from the U.S.?ORDOÑEZ: Yeah, I mean, very much designed to demonstrate American power, but I also think it does show that power and influence are not the same thing. I mean, Trump was asked today if Putin, who he called his friend, was also America's friend.(SOUNDBITE OF ARCHIVED RECORDING)TRUMP: I can't speak to America.ORDOÑEZ: You know, he really couldn't answer that. But he did continue to make the case that his relationship with Putin would reap benefits for America, though we haven't really seen that yet. You know, the war in Ukraine continues to rage on. But we are seeing allies start to build alliances with other nations as, you know, confidence in the U.S. falters, and they look to reduce their dependence on the U.S.CHANG: Well, great. What about progress when it comes to Iran? Did anything come out of this trip on that front?MYRE: The short answer is no. There's no indication the war, now nearly nine months old, was discussed in any great detail on the trip. Trump did mention it briefly at the news conference. He said what he said many times before - Iran can't have a nuclear weapon and that Iran does want to make a deal. The one significant development in recent days has been increased Iranian attacks on oil tankers and Gulf countries.CHANG: OK, Franco, real quick on domestic politics. Now, Trump was up there with Vice President Vance - right? - and Secretary of State Marco Rubio. Anything strike you about what either of those men said?ORDOÑEZ: Well, I mean, both men offered really glowing support for the president. And Vance, who obviously remained in Washington for the trip, said he missed the president and even joked that he felt like he was in the movie "Home Alone."CHANG: (Laughter).ORDOÑEZ: Whereas Rubio was able to talk more authoritatively about his work and just came across as a more consequential figure. The issue for both, though, is that their association with Trump, who is, frankly, very unpopular now.CHANG: That is NPR's Franco Ordoñez and NPR's Greg Myre. Thank you to both of you.ORDOÑEZ: (Inaudible).MYRE: Sure thing, Ailsa.

title: Week in Politics: Trump returns from Asia; hails trip as one of best in history
description: President Trump returned from his trip to Asia, saying it was one of the most successful presidential visits to that continent — or anywhere el
body:
President Trump returned from his trip to Asia, saying it was one of the most successful presidential visits to that continent — or anywhere else — in American history.   

    
        
          Transcript
        
    SCOTT SIMON, HOST:  In China, this week, President Trump attended the first-ever trilateral meeting with the leaders of China and Russia. Some commentators compared it to the 1945 Yalta Conference, where post-war leaders divided Eastern Europe.(SOUNDBITE OF ARCHIVED RECORDING)PRESIDENT DONALD TRUMP: I didn't go having us talk about Yalta, and if you look, Winston Churchill, Stalin, FDR - which was a big one - I didn't think about it. I just went saying, I get along great with these two people. We'll work out our differences. We've been able to work them out. And all of a sudden, I see you people talking it's the biggest but - and then I realized how big it was. It was an amazing event.SIMON: President Trump during an hour-and-a-half-long press conference yesterday at the White House. NPR Senior contributor Ron Elving joins us. Ron, thanks so much for being with us.RON ELVING, BYLINE: Good to be with you, Scott.SIMON: What do you make of this meeting, President Trump with China's Xi Jinping and Russia's Vladimir Putin all seated around a big round table?ELVING: Yes, an enormous circular table - to some degree, a symbol of equality among the three men, but still staged to place Chinese President Xi as host. We know that President Trump cares a lot about visuals and staging, and here we had perhaps the most elaborate photo opportunity in history. If you watched the news conference yesterday as a Trump admirer, you got plenty to feed that. Otherwise, you could have felt the claims of peacemaking and dealmaking in Asia were long on promise and woefully short on details.When asked yesterday whether his friend Putin was a friend to America, Trump said he could not speak to America, a remarkable thing for a president to say. Then he went back to when Putin denied colluding with Trump's first campaign in 2016, saying how much he had appreciated Putin's support in that episode. Ukraine's leader, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, responded last night several hours later, saying for Ukraine, Putin was not a friend, but a killer using terrorism against civilians.SIMON: Ron, any appearances aside, does a meeting like this have consequences - real-world consequences?ELVING: It could have if these various vows of peaceful cooperation bear fruit, or if these vaunted trade deals come to pass. But what we do know at this point is that Russia this week launched one of its most massive assaults against Ukraine since it first invaded that country in 2022, assaults against civilian targets that also struck Poland, a NATO ally of the U.S. And it makes a difference that Trump was more interested in meeting with Chinese President Xi than he was in confronting that country's efforts to obtain the most advanced American computer chips.SIMON: On a question about the Democrats, Hakeem Jeffries on track to be speaker of the House in January. On the Senate side, Senator Chuck Schumer faces a challenge. What are you watching for?ELVING: Jeffries is now the official Democratic nominee. He got 251 votes out of 262 cast - way more than he'll need to be formally elected in January. The last time, when Nancy Pelosi was nominated for speaker, she barely got over 200 votes and had to do some heavy lifting to bring her dissidents on board. Jeffries, from the start, can concentrate on Trump and the Republicans from a secure position.Now, the Democrats in the Senate have yet to vote, and the presumed leader there - another New Yorker, Chuck Schumer - has a long history in leadership and perhaps too much baggage for younger Democrats. Chris Van Hollen of Maryland has challenged him and promises a fresh face. But so far, if there's a big move to Van Hollen happening among Senate Democrats, it remains below the surface.SIMON: And finally, Elon Musk - richest person in the world, biggest spender of the midterms - now says he's not MAGA.ELVING: Yes. You may recall his red ball cap that said Trump was right about everything. So maybe not so right about Elon Musk. His promise to cut trillions from the federal budget fizzled. Then he dropped something approaching half a billion dollars on the midterms and got shut out. He is a brilliant engineer and businessman, to be sure, but that does not always translate to success in politics. Republicans won't miss him on the campaign trail if he's really through with it, but they may well miss that money.SIMON: NPR's Ron Elving. Thanks so much.ELVING: Thank you, Scott.

title: Politics chat: Lawmakers step up with only weeks to Democrats' control of Congress
description: A funding deadline for Congress weeks before Democrats take control. President Trump signs an executive order requiring contractors to get appr
body:
A funding deadline for Congress weeks before Democrats take control. President Trump signs an executive order requiring contractors to get approval before sharing with Congressional investigations.   

    
        
          Transcript
        
    AYESHA RASCOE, HOST:  President Trump is expected to head to Mar-a-Lago this week for Thanksgiving. But Congress is already on recess. When lawmakers return, there will be plenty for them to do with just weeks to go before Democrats take control of both chambers. Joining me now in studio is NPR congressional reporter Eric McDaniel. Good morning, Eric.ERIC MCDANIEL, BYLINE: Hey there.RASCOE: There is a funding deadline coming up on December 11. The president is demanding $350 billion in new defense spending. Funding deadlines and Congress always make people think about, is there going to be a shutdown? How likely is it that lawmakers don't come to an agreement in time?MCDANIEL: I mean, it's definitely possible that we see a government shutdown. I don't think we'll see 350 billion in new Pentagon spending, but I want to remind people that lawmakers are aware of the stakes here. Like you were pointing out, the federal government is the nation's largest employer, and we're coming off an election where the public just rebuked a Congress that dragged it through the longest shutdown in U.S. history.Some 90% of the public believes that the government is corrupt, that lawmakers advocate for their own self-interests rather than the public. They connect that back to a high cost of living. Plus, right now, Democrats are loath to fund the president's unpopular war in Iran, but they don't have full control until January. And so the calculus might be a short-term money for, you know, keeping their powder dry until the new year.RASCOE: And two outgoing Senate Republicans have also blocked Trump's nominees for various jobs. John Cornyn of Texas blocked an official from the Justice Department from a seat on a U.S. district court, and North Carolina's Thom Tillis blocked two nominees, one for a key U.S. cybersecurity agency and another to lead the Government Accountability Office. Tell us more about that last one.MCDANIEL: Yeah, the Government Accountability Office. This is a big deal. And in a lot of ways, the consequence is the president alienating so many lawmakers from his own party, right? Let's focus on the GAO. This accountability branch helps Congress with their oversight responsibilities. That's a key constitutional obligation they have. Trump and allies were trying to install a figure Democrats, and some Republicans, like you mentioned, viewed as too partisan.But the other issue for lawmakers was that it's another example of the White House and executive branch trying to yank control away from Congress, which has happened on everything from the power of the purse to the power to declare war. And I think in this environment, that power grab just wasn't going to fly. Still, it isn't as though Senate Republicans aren't going to do any confirmations, right? They will be laser-focused on confirming as many judges and other Cabinet - not Cabinet appointees - other presidential appointees, like ambassadors, before they lose their gavels in January.RASCOE: Well, speaking of that, you know, the White House trying to wrest control...MCDANIEL: Yeah.RASCOE: ...From Congress. Democrats are planning to launch any number of investigations once they take charge. On Friday, the president issued this new executive order that bars federal contractors from sharing information with Congress without instructions from the White House. Does this executive order have any teeth?MCDANIEL: Look, I'm not a lawyer. I'm not that smart. But I'll let them sort out the details. I do want to make one big point. The White House can do anything they want to try and prevent people from complying with the legal investigatory powers of Congress. But everyone, particularly if they're outside of government, is taking individual legal risk that the administration can't really insulate them from. That's legal bills. That's time. That's a potential contempt of Congress vote, reputational cost. And all of this is pretty high stakes, right? Getting dragged before Congress is no small thing.And remember what incoming House Oversight Committee chairman Robert Garcia, a Democrat, posted when Democrats had won the majority. He said, lawyer up. So his party and all of their investigatory committees aren't going to be timid at all at pursuing their legal avenues, no matter what executive orders the president issues.RASCOE: That's NPR congressional reporter Eric McDaniel. Thank you so much.MCDANIEL: Thanks, Ayesha.

title: Christian nationalist conference hosts Nick Fuentes, vows to keep pushing MAGA agenda
description: A particular group of Christian nationalists met in Texas last weekend and vowed to push what remains of MAGA as far to the right as possible.
body:
A particular group of Christian nationalists met in Texas last weekend and vowed to push what remains of MAGA as far to the right as possible. They hosted antisemitic streamer Nick Fuentes.   

    
        
          Transcript
        
    AYESHA RASCOE, HOST:  The midterm election results have some people writing obituaries for the MAGA movement. But last weekend, a particular faction of Christian nationalists got together in Dallas with a plan to push what's left of Trump's coalition as far to the right as possible. NPR's Lisa Hagen was there. And a note - her story contains antisemitic, racist and misogynistic language.(SOUNDBITE OF ARCHIVED RECORDING)JOEL WEBBON: I'm not demoralized. I'm not defeated, and neither should you be. There will be an America after Trump.LISA HAGEN, BYLINE: That's Joel Webbon, a pastor from Texas and the man who's organized this event called Christ is King: America after Trump. Webbon's reach on the Christian right has been growing. And this moment, this gathering in Dallas, is another big step for him. Several national news outlets are here. The event has drawn about a thousand attendees. The vast majority are white men. A lot of them are in their 30s and 40s, some with meticulously coiffed beards and mustaches.(SOUNDBITE OF ARCHIVED RECORDING)WEBBON: Most of you are right-wing. God bless you. Right? You're going to disagree with me because it's like - Joel Webbon's kind of embarrassing. I mean, he's to the left of George Washington. What's the guy even doing?HAGEN: That's a little joke Webbon likes to use because Washington owned slaves. Webbon claims he believes that there are at least some Black men in America who should retain the right to vote. The conference was filled with similar statements from Webbon and other speakers, which is exactly what the attendees have come to hear for three straight days.(SOUNDBITE OF ARCHIVED RECORDING)WEBBON: It's not just OK to be white. It's good to be white. Praise God.HAGEN: Another of Webbon's favorite talking points is repealing women's right to vote, as well as eliminating their place in public life.(SOUNDBITE OF ARCHIVED RECORDING)WEBBON: Every time you see a woman in leadership, I guarantee there were at least a thousand men who were more qualified for that position than her.HAGEN: And to top it all off, overt antisemitism.(SOUNDBITE OF ARCHIVED RECORDING)WEBBON: I'm not trying to be a jerk about this or overly edgy, but the leading cause of the rise of antisemitism remains kind of Jewish behavior.HAGEN: Webbon is not the pastor of a megachurch. His actual congregation near Austin has about 200 people. But his profile online has spiked as his messages about race, women and Jews have gotten more explicit. He got a big boost earlier this year as he began hosting Nick Fuentes, a 28-year-old far-right streamer and self-described racist and antisemite who's advocated for raping women.The general branch of Christianity that Webbon is a part of, who call themselves Reformed, is a pretty small group. It's an estimated 2% of Christians in America. But Kristin Kobes Du Mez, a history professor at Calvin University, says she worries that Webbon's influence has begun to break containment from that small Reformed community.KRISTIN KOBES DU MEZ: Reformed is a Protestant denomination going back to both Martin Luther and especially John Calvin. And the idea that to be a faithful Christian is to shape the rest of society around God's norms - when you accomplish that, then you're going to flourish.HAGEN: Du Mez herself is Reformed, and she says some in the denomination interpret their religious purpose as the pursuit of social justice. But she says the Joel Webbon branch tends to take what she calls a more coercive approach.DU MEZ: As a mandate to seize control over all sectors of life and to really freeze out anybody of a different religious faith or of a Christian faith that doesn't align with their understanding, to freeze them out of all positions of power and influence - this is what they mean when they say Christ is king.(SOUNDBITE OF ARCHIVED RECORDING)UNIDENTIFIED CROWD: (Chanting) Christ is king. Christ is king. Christ is king.HAGEN: Evangelicals, like everyone else, exist across a political spectrum. But Du Mez says they often share biblical language and phrases. And she says figures like Webbon use that common language to promote very far-right interpretations. Du Mez says she's been watching the more extreme versions of Reformed theology begin to spread, usually through men, across the community and beyond.DU MEZ: Things that seemed unacceptable before become, at first, controversial - you know, part of the conversation - and then increasingly become kind of acceptable and even the norm.HAGEN: One of the young men we met at the conference, in his early 20s, said he got into some of these ideas after a friend introduced him to music by one of the event's speakers. It became really special to him. And he sang a few lines for us.C: (Singing) Don't give any heed to cowardly tongues. There's glory out there, out there to be won.Oh, so good.HAGEN: He asked that NPR refer to him by his last initial, C, because he doesn't want to be associated with a specific conference speaker. C has gone to the same church all his life, one with women pastors. But as he's listened more to Webbon and podcasters like him, he's started worrying that's wrong.C: And so I'm kind of in the phase right now of asking questions - like, asking the men who are the foundation of the church, like, what does Scripture say? And how should we handle these things?HAGEN: He says some of the elders have told him privately that they agree women shouldn't lead churches, but getting rid of them might drive people away from the message of Jesus. And that's really the tension at the heart of this whole conference. It is outspoken racism, antisemitism and misogyny that Webbon has used to draw this crowd. A majority of his most popular podcast and video episodes have been the ones that feature that antisemitic streamer, Nick Fuentes, who ended up being the surprise special guest Webbon invited to close out his conference.(SOUNDBITE OF ARCHIVED RECORDING)NICK FUENTES: You'll find that throughout history, it is a small group of highly motivated people that change the world. It's a small group of fanatics, zealots, the martyrs, the people that are willing to die for what they believe in. That's us. That's the people in this room.HAGEN: Fuentes rarely speaks to live audiences, but he had this one on its feet.(SOUNDBITE OF ARCHIVED RECORDING)FUENTES: Thank you. God bless you. Goodnight.(CHEERING)HAGEN: He and Webbon don't agree on everything. Webbon thinks it may take longer than the next two years to gain enough traction to take power, which he's talked about on his podcast.(SOUNDBITE OF ARCHIVED RECORDING)WEBBON: Our plan does not require a majority vote. So when I say we will win, I'm not saying that we will win through democracy.HAGEN: Both Webbon and Fuentes are young. So are a lot of their followers, and they're all counting on being the future of the right.Lisa Hagen, NPR News.(SOUNDBITE OF LINHY'S "RADIANCE")

title: An effort to circumvent the Electoral College may be within reach. But hurdles remain
description: Voting booths are seen at Glass Elementa
body:
Voting booths are seen at Glass Elementary School's polling station in Eagle Pass, Texas, on Nov. 8, 2022.
                
                    Mark Felix/AFP via Getty Images
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Mark Felix/AFP via Getty Images
    

   
   A national effort to ensure that only winners of the popular vote become president could reach a critical milestone soon.   It's a possible outcome of huge Democratic wins in this month's midterm elections.   Next year, Democrats will fully control five states that could sign the National Popular Vote Interstate Compact, an agreement among states to award their presidential electoral votes to the winner of the nationwide popular vote, not the winner of their respective states.    
   If they do join other 18 Democratic-led states — plus the District of Columbia — that are in the compact, the effort will have surpassed the needed 270 electoral votes required to go into effect, making an end run around the Electoral College. So far no Republican-led states have joined the compact and the party is largely not unified on the issue.   There are still plenty of political, practical and legal hurdles that this effort would need to clear. But proponents are optimistic many of those hurdles will be cleared – even perhaps in time for the next presidential election.   "I've never been more confident that 63% of American voters can get what they want in the 2028 presidential election, which is a national popular vote for president." Patrick Rosenstiel, a senior consultant to National Popular Vote, the group pushing for the compact in states across the country, told NPR, referencing Pew polling.   Right now, the compact has a total of 222 electoral votes. The five states that will soon be completely in the hands of Democrats – Arizona, Pennsylvania, Michigan, Nevada and Wisconsin – add up to 61 electoral votes. Combinations of at least four of those states would put the compact over 270.   So far, governors and incoming governors in Pennsylvania and Nevada have said they are open to signing legislation that would bring their states into the interstate agreement. But other governors have yet to publicly weigh in.   
   One of the looming questions over these efforts is whether these states – all presidential battlegrounds – would be willing to give up their immense influence in elections ahead of the 2028 presidential contests.   And leaders in each state will also have to weigh whether they want to be the tipping point in moving forward a movement that could upend how the U.S. decides presidential winners.   Already, some Democrats are more reticent on the issue than they were before. For example, Democratic Arizona Gov. Katie Hobbs, who had previously supported the measure, has not commented recently on whether the state's new Democratic majorities should sign on. NPR reached out to Hobbs' office for comment but did not receive a response before publication.   And then of course, there are the various legal and logistical hurdles.    The practical and legal hurdles   Some legal scholars have observed that this agreement between states could run afoul of the compact clause in the Constitution, which says that "no state shall, without the consent of Congress … enter into any agreement or compact with another state … unless actually invaded, or in such imminent danger as will not admit of delay."   Norman Williams, a constitutional law professor at Willamette University, said that beyond the legal hurdles, he sees a range of practical issues with the compact.   Mostly, he said, it could upend what is a core feature of American presidential elections, which is that they are largely decentralized.   States individually decide who can vote and how they can vote. He said forcing electors from one state to vote according to the tallies in another state could create some tension.   "We would want to have a standardized, uniform set of rules regarding who gets to vote for president, how they vote, how those votes are tabulated, and to have a federal election authority doing that tabulation," he said. "I think trying to nationalize [the current system] and entrusting a national election to 51 separate election administrators would just sow discord and distrust."   
   But John Koza, the chairman of National Popular Vote, said if the compact works the way it is supposed to, none of that will be necessary.   
   "We don't need a centralized bureaucracy or a presidentially appointed commission that could be manipulated," he told NPR. "The simple fact is current state and federal law provide for the issuance of a certified vote count from each state. And all that has to be done is add them up."   But mostly, Williams said the biggest question before this effort is whether such a large reform should be done via a constitutional amendment.   Upending the Electoral College, some argue, would be a profound change to how the U.S. chooses the leader of the free world. Opponents of a national popular vote, such as Save Our States, argue that without the incentives created by the Electoral College, American politics will move more toward "toward more regional politics and would exacerbate existing divides."   Williams said even though it will be much more difficult to pull off, it would be worth going through a more fulsome process via Article 5 to get rid of the Electoral College, instead of working around it.   "This is where I think process matters," he said. "If you really want to have a national popular vote for the president and avoid all of the legal and practical difficulties, you need to do that through a constitutional amendment, because only a constitutional amendment can address the legal and practical challenges of conducting a national popular vote for the presidency."   A similar effort to pass an amendment to get rid of the Electoral College in 1969 failed, though. And very few amendments have even gotten close to passing in recent history.   Rosenstiel, the consultant to the National Popular Vote, said this is why he thinks groups like his are seeking a creative solution to something most Americans agree is a problem.   
   And, he said, he ultimately thinks a national popular vote will solve multiple problems at once. For one, he said, it will force presidential candidates to appeal to most of the country, as opposed to a select group of voters in battleground states.   And, importantly, he said, it would make all voters feel like their vote matters.   "We should have a system where every American citizen feels valued and is valued when they cast their vote," he said. "And there's only one reform that delivers it."

title: The New Yorker's Jason Zengerle on Hakeem Jeffries' rise to first Black House speaker
description: Hakeem Jeffries is set to become the first-ever African American speaker of the U.S. House of Representatives. NPR's Scott Simon talks to Jason
body:
Hakeem Jeffries is set to become the first-ever African American speaker of the U.S. House of Representatives. NPR's Scott Simon talks to Jason Zengerle of The New Yorker about the rise of Jeffries.   

    
        
          Transcript
        
    SCOTT SIMON, HOST:  Hakeem Jeffries is poised to make history - the first African American speaker of the House of Representatives. House Democrats nominated him for the post on Wednesday, all but guaranteeing his election when the new Congress takes power in January. Jeffries said voters had sent a clear message on Election Day.(SOUNDBITE OF ARCHIVED RECORDING)HAKEEM JEFFRIES: We hear you. We see you. We feel you. And House Democrats are committed to making life better for you.SIMON: So how is the new speaker going to lead? Jason Zengerle covers politics for The New Yorker, and he has profiled Hakeem Jeffries. He joins us now from Chapel Hill, North Carolina. Mr. Zengerle, thanks so much for being with us.JASON ZENGERLE: Thanks for having me on.SIMON: How would you describe Hakeem Jeffries and his politics?ZENGERLE: He is a very careful, deliberate, strategic politician. He is the opposite of impulsive. He has extreme message discipline. And he's been very careful to, you know, avoid getting ideologically pigeonholed.SIMON: He was a corporate litigator at one point in his life, wasn't he?ZENGERLE: Yeah. He was a white-shoe lawyer, worked at Paul, Weiss. And then went to work in-house at CBS and he would have had a very successful career. But he was very insistent that he wanted to run for office. He was really interested in local New York City politics. He'd grown up in Brooklyn. And he really wanted to do that.SIMON: His faith means a lot to him, doesn't it?ZENGERLE: Yeah. He grew up in Brooklyn. And his mother was a Sunday school teacher at a church called Cornerstone Baptist, which is in Bedford-Stuyvesant. It's one of the more prominent Black Baptist churches in Brooklyn. And, you know, from a young age, he was an usher at the church. He was - you know, he got really used to speaking to large crowds. And his faith is really important to him. When I was doing the story, you know, the most sort of enjoyable time I spent with him was a morning in Brooklyn where he was going to various church services. He tries to go to, I think, about a hundred a year. He was just so much more relaxed and so much more kind of in his element than when I spent time with him in Washington.SIMON: Well, how would you characterize his leadership style?ZENGERLE: You know, he once said to me that, you know, the most important words that he could say to any member of Congress on any issue were, what do you think? And I think that he views his job as listening and then trying to formulate strategy from that. You know, there are people in the Democratic caucus who feel that he needs to be tougher and tell members, you know, you need to vote this way. They want him to give more guidance. I think there's a feeling that oftentimes he doesn't want to give that guidance because he doesn't want to make members mad at him.SIMON: I have to ask. In this day and age, does guidance work anymore? There are so many different forces.ZENGERLE: That's a good question. I mean, that's a very good question, you know. Like, would they listen to him even if he said, you have to do this? And I think that's part of his strategy is that I think he feels that if they feel like they're being listened to, they're more likely going to come around to his way of thinking.SIMON: He will become speaker with a very large majority. But also a president who is likely to veto most everything. How does he maneuver that?ZENGERLE: Well, I think for the next couple years, you know, his job and Democrats on Capitol Hill, their job is going to be to pass a series of messaging bills. They don't expect Donald Trump to agree with them on lowering the age for Medicare or, you know, raising the minimum wage. But they want to pass this legislation so that whoever the Democratic presidential nominee is in 2028 can run on the campaign of saying, look at what Congress passed. Look at what Donald Trump vetoed. If you put a Democrat in the White House, all of these things will become law.SIMON: Can you tell so far how he's likely to be on the question of investigations into the Trump administration?ZENGERLE: I think that's one area where Democrats actually can do a good amount. And I think he's going to be very aggressive there. I think that he and the two sort of Democrats who'll be in charge of oversight or most involved in it - Jamie Raskin of Judiciary Committee and Robert Garcia at House Oversight - he's been coordinating with them long before the midterms, talking about who will be the targets of investigations. And that's something that, you know, Democrats were very aggressive with back in 2019, the last time they took back the House when Donald Trump was president.SIMON: Will support for or criticism of Israel test his leadership?ZENGERLE: When I said earlier that he tries not to be identified with certain issues, you know, ironically, Israel is one issue in which he is strongly identified with. He has been a strong supporter of Israel throughout his career. You know, when he came to Washington, his support for Israel was very much within the mainstream of the Democratic Party. But support for Israel has really declined within the Democratic Party since then. And he himself, I think, has moved a little bit in the direction of critics of Israel. But he hasn't moved as far as a lot of people in the party, and I think that's going to be a real flashpoint.SIMON: What are some of the biggest challenges the speaker will face?ZENGERLE: You know, just keeping his caucus together. When you're in the minority, it's much easier to keep your caucus together. And it's especially easy when Donald Trump is the president. Everybody can rally around him. Now that they're actually going to be able to pass legislation, you know, he's going to have more intraparty conflict on, you know, not only Israel, but on healthcare and other issues. And he's going to have to try to manage those tensions.SIMON: Jason Zengerle, who writes about politics for The New Yorker, thanks so much for being with us.ZENGERLE: Thanks a lot for having me.(SOUNDBITE OF THE QUANTIC SOUL ORCHESTRA & QUANTIC'S "FATHER")
